articles.sourceTitle: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
articles.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
articles.text:
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks, the ubiquity of these devices has made the company’s education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google’s new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. There’s no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.
This is actually consistent with Google’s approach in the consumer space. Google executives have said in no uncertain terms that Google Search is AI search. Most searches now provide an AI Overview at the top, and the company is constantly coming up with new ways to nudge people toward the conversational AI Mode chatbot function. Google sees this as the future.

articles.sourceTitle: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
articles.title: [SEVERE] Desktop auto-installs Codex/Claude plugins; installer attempts to trust its own startup hook #14370
articles.text:
Is there an existing issue for this?

I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed

Describe the Issue
Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.
I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it.
Evidence from this Mac
Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026.
1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation
From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time):

PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"}

Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"}

2. Codex's global user configuration was changed
Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml:

[marketplaces.postman]
source_type = "git"
source = "https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git"

[plugins."postman@postman"]
enabled = true

[hooks.state."postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks.json:session_start:0:0"]
trusted_hash = "sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3"
trusted_content_hash = "sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345"

3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman
The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including:

Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the postman:api-engineer skill and follow it.

That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman.
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md

Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json
4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook
installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation".
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts

Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts
The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction.
5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection
mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp. Codex logs contain:

MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request

Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/mcp.codex.json
6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI
~/.claude/settings.json enabled postman@claude-plugins-official. ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json recorded version 2.0.1, user scope, installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. A Postman executable and its lib directory were present in ~/.local/bin, with modification times matching the installation window.
Private paths, unrelated logs, account identifiers, and credentials are excluded. This report establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes; it does not claim to establish data exfiltration.
Steps To Reproduce
Observed sequence (not yet reproduced on a clean Mac):

Open an existing Postman desktop installation after not using it for a while.
Postman's log records auto-existing-upgrade and successful Codex/Claude installation.
Start Codex. Observe Postman MCP authentication failures and API tasks loading Postman skills.
Inspect the global user config, cached plugin hooks, installer source, and Claude install records described above.

Expected: installing plugins, adding remote connections, and trusting hooks in other applications each require a clear, specific opt-in in the affected application.

Actual: the integrations were installed automatically and broad startup instructions were added.
Screenshots or Videos
No response
Operating System
macOS
Postman Version
12.33.4 (Codex plugin 1.1.0; Claude plugin 2.0.1)
Postman Platform
Postman App
User Account Type
Signed In User
Additional Context?
Requested response:

Treat this as a severe product consent and security-boundary incident, not a documentation question.
Stop automatic agent-plugin/CLI installation for existing desktop users pending explicit opt-in.
Remove installer-side self-approval of hooks. Hook trust must be decided by the user in the agent host.
Identify the exact release/feature flag and consent flow behind auto-existing-upgrade, including which other agents and files can be changed.
Provide a complete rollback/uninstall path covering agent configs, hook trust, marketplaces, caches, MCP connections, and the CLI; respect removal without reinstalling.
Narrow startup skill instructions to explicit Postman requests rather than making Postman the default for general API engineering.

I have removed the local Postman installation and integrations after preserving the evidence. The source links are pinned to the exact locally installed Codex plugin revision. I am requesting maintainer triage at severe priority; I cannot assign repository labels myself.

Reacted by Rafael Wolf, Manuel Schnidrig, Shane Saunders, aaron-au, Angus Tang, Shawn Stawiarski, Neil Menne, Wayne Durack, Aaron Triplett, Jiaxiang Zhang and 57 more

Reacted by Giuseppe La Malfa, ZeroHackz and Dom Hallan

articles.sourceTitle: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
articles.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat – Terence Eden’s Blog
articles.text:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:

Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day

I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.
Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.
I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit, I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.
I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:

I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!
Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it.
I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.
Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.

Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.
I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.
But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.
It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

articles.sourceTitle: AI is destroying my CS degree
articles.title: AI is destroying my CS degree – who even knows
articles.text:
AI is destroying my CS degree

03 Nov, 2026

I am a computer science student. I got a scholarship to study computer science and AI last year and I love it! It's something that I wanted to do since I was a kid but couldn't afford it.
It's been a huge learning curve. I only had a B in maths from GCSE (which is the exam you take at 16 for non UK folk) and no technical training other than the funny little games I made on OpenProcessing*.
Regardless of how hard it's been, I have enjoyed the challenge. I wouldn't have signed up to study computing if I thought it would be an easy ride. The problem is that my university seems to be having an existential crisis because of AI, and it's making the experience much shittier than it was before.
The flip flopping makes everything uncertainDuring my studies, my uni has flip flopped between YOU MUST NEVER USE AI and YOU MUST USE AI and also YES WE'RE USING AI BUT THAT DOESN'T MEAN YOU SHOULD!
They seem to have made an art of choosing the worst possible use cases for AI (marking and feedback, course content creation, and student engagement emails) and going all in on them, only to roll back the decision 3 months later. Students are mandated to use AI in assignments, only to reach the next module where you lose marks for even touching an LLM.
Coursework design has gone down the toiletI mean, it was never perfect to begin with. Assessing skill in computer science is a difficult problem to solve, but getting Claude to crank out bloated assessment briefs is not the solution. Whereas before, assignments were designed by a person who thought them through at least once, then approved by other people in the department, now I doubt they're getting read more than once (if that). Errors abound, often with corrections coming a week or two before the deadline.
The amount of work involved has also tripled - LLMs don't know how much effort it takes for a student to learn new material then complete technical tasks, and professors are too far along in their careers to notice this when skim reading an AI generated brief. So those of us with less technical experience are forced to speed run content, which SUCKS! I am here to learn, god damn it, not barely scratch the surface of the 15 deliverables I have for a 3,000 word assignment.
Tutors are overloaded (even more than usual)You know what university financiers love to hear? SCALE! Learning at scale, preferable automated, so they can milk the cash cow as much as possible without paying for extra staff. There has always been tension between educational and commercial interests in every institution, but the AI hype has forced through a level of workload that is unethical and unsustainable for tutors and lecturers. I only hear from my tutor these days when I haven't accessed the online portal in a while, because their data dashboard flagged me as 'at risk' T_T
Doomers left, right and centreI don't care if computer science and maths are over! I still want to learn about them! OK, I do care about my future career, but it still doesn't mean I want to forget everything I learned or stop progressing on this journey. There are so many interesting avenues to explore (some AI, some not), but I can't move for headlines about how software engineering is over/not using AI makes you obsolete/blah blah blah. Can't a girl learn statistics for fun?
I could go on, but I won't. It'll give me indigestion. Maybe I'll go back to OpenProcessing for a bit and make some more silly games now I actually know how to do a bit of programming.

Give em a go! Click in the browser frame to activate keyboard controls.

articles.sourceTitle: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
articles.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public
articles.text: Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense: they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts, Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s marginsKey forces squeezing the AI industry’s marginsAI industry marginsDemand pressure:Businesses and consumersmay not be willing to payenough for generative AI.Commoditization:Fierce competitionwill make it difficult toraise prices.Cost pressures:High costs mean developerscan’t cut prices withouthemorrhaging cash.External constraints:Supply-chain challenges andcommunity opposition drive upcosts and delay revenue generation.AI industry marginsDemand pressure:Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI.Commoditization:Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices.Cost pressures:High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash.External constraints:Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation.First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies, including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid.Our content delivered to your inbox.Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracyThank you!You have successfully joined our subscriber list.Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion, and the prices for some components are soaring.That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect.” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy.
